nodes.summary: A group $G$ has a unique product presentation if there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and elements $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in G$ such that every element of $G$ equals $a_0^{k_0} a_1^{k_1} \cdots a_{n-1}^{k_{n-1}}$ for exactly one tuple $(k_0, \dots, k_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{Z}^n$.
nodes.title: Groups with a unique product presentation

nodes.summary: A group $G$ is almost polycyclic, or virtually polycyclic, if some subgroup of finite index in $G$ is polycyclic.
nodes.title: Almost polycyclic groups (Kourovka Problem 13.11)

nodes.summary: A group $G$ is polycyclic if it has a finite series of subgroups $1 = H_0 \le H_1 \le \cdots \le H_n = G$ in which each $H_i$ is normal in $H_{i+1}$ and each quotient $H_{i+1} / H_i$ is cyclic.
nodes.title: Polycyclic groups (Kourovka Problem 13.11)

nodes.summary: Not every torsion-free group with a unique product presentation is almost polycyclic: there is a group $G$ in which no element other than $1$ has finite order, which has a unique product presentation, and which is not almost polycyclic.
nodes.title: A torsion-free group with a unique product presentation need not be almost polycyclic

nodes.summary: The statement, asked by V. V. Bludov, that every group $G$ which is torsion-free (no element of $G$ other than $1$ has finite order) and has a unique product presentation is almost polycyclic.
nodes.title: Kourovka Problem 13.11 (torsion-free groups with a unique product presentation)
